title: hbcLock: Encrypted RF Communication Utilizing Body-Coupled Keys for the Internet of Bodies
problem: Wearable devices transmitting sensitive health data via RF (BLE, Wi-Fi) face eavesdropping risks. Traditional encryption key management is cumbersome and insecure for implanted or wearable bioelectronics.
motivation: Internet of Bodies (IoB) applications require both secure RF communication and practical key establishment. Body-coupled communications can leverage the human body as an implicit authentication channel.
method: The wearable encrypts health data (such as ECG signals) using a secret key and broadcasts the encrypted data wirelessly over RF channels like Bluetooth or Wi-Fi. Simultaneously, it sends the unencrypted key through the wearer's body tissue using a human body communication channel—electrical signals that only travel through direct skin contact when touched. Only a receiver in direct physical contact captures the key this way, while the encrypted data broadcasts to anyone in RF range. The intended receiver combines the key received through body contact with the wireless-received data to decrypt the health information.
key_novelty: The innovation is using human body tissue as the encryption-key distribution channel while sending encrypted health data wirelessly, so only an authorized person touching the device can decrypt the transmitted data.
contributions: Proof-of-concept hbcLock system with custom wearable and receiver
1-lead ECG encryption and transmission via BLE with parallel body-coupled key transfer
100% match achieved between decrypted ECG and original signal
Preliminary characterization of human body channel quality for key transfer
limitations: Limited to 1-lead ECG; scalability to multi-channel bioelectronics unclear
Human body channel characterization preliminary; long-term reliability and attenuation unknown
Threat model assumes proximity-based contact; distant eavesdropping not addressed
No formal security analysis or penetration testing results provided
Power consumption and form factor constraints not discussed
